Multiple hydrogen bond coordination in three- constituent deep eutectic solvents enhances lignin fractionation from biomass†
Qinqin Xia, Yongzhuang Liu, Juan Meng, Wanke Cheng, Wenshuai Chen, Shouxin Liu, ID Yixing Liu, Jian Li and Haipeng Yu ID *

As an emerging generation of green solvents, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are promising for the pre-treatment of lignocellulose and the production of biochemicals. However, not all DESs are effective for the cleavage of lignin–carbohydrate complexes (LCCs) in lignocellulose and the fractionation of lignin. In this study, we analyzed the nature of complex molecular interactions between choline chloride (ChCl) and glycerol in ChCl/glycerol (1:2) DES using density functional theory and the Kamlet–Taft solvatochro-mic method. The ChCl–glycerol DES exhibited weak competing interactions towards the linkages in the LCC network because the intramolecular hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) in ChCl–glycerol were constrained by mutually anionic H-bonds ([Cl(glycerol)]⁻) and cationic H-bonds ([Ch(glycerol)]⁺). Furthermore, because of the absence of active protons and acidic sites, the DES was unable to cleave ether bond lin-kages in the LCCs. Accordingly, we designed a three-constituent DES (3c-DES) by coordinating AlCl₃·6H₂O in ChCl/glycerol DES based on an acidic multisite coordination theory. The competition of anionic H-bonds and unidentate aluminum ligands was synchronized to form supramolecular complexes, allowing the multisite bridging ligands to cleave both the H-bonds and ether bonds in LCCs. Consequently, the lignin fractionation efficiency was significantly improved from 3.61% to 95.46%, and the lignin purity reached 94 ± 0.45%.

With the depletion of fossil energy resources, biomass utilization is of significant importance for the production of alternative renewables.¹ Recently, the biomass pretreatment efficiency has been improved with the development and better understanding of novel solvents that do not harm the environment and are compatible with nature.² Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as a promising new generation of green solvents which fully accord with the 12 principles of green chemistry. They are inexpensive, easy to prepare, nontoxic, biodegradable, and environmentally friendly.³ Compared with toxic solvents and expensive solvents, DESs can be used in lieu of conventional chemical solvents and have a low ecological footprint.

Some acidic DESs that show an efficient lignin extraction ability have been reported. However, not all types of DESs can be applied to biomass fractionation. Glycerol, as a natural compound and the main by-product generated by the biodiesel

Glycerol-based DESs have been prepared as easily accessible, biodegradable, and inexpensive alternatives to conventional aprotic cation-anion paired ionic liquids.⁶ Glycerol-based DESs displayed excellent fluidity coupled with high thermal stability, and are effective in the electrochemical deposition of metal films or the extraction of active ingredients.⁷ However, glycerol-based DESs have been frequently reported to be less effective for biomass fractionation. For example, a choline chloride (ChCl) and glycerol (ChCl/glycerol) DES was used to dissolve corncobs at 115 °C for 15 h, but it only showed a low lignin solubility of 4.4%.⁸ Alvarez-Vasco et al. reported that the removal of lignin in Douglas fir and poplar was difficult after pretreatment with ChCl/glycerol DES.⁹ Fang et al. also reported that ChCl/glycerol DES had little effect on removing the lignin from date palm residues.¹⁰ It is still not well understood how the nature of the interactions between the organic matter and the ChCl/glycerol DES affect the biomass fractionation.¹¹ Therefore, an in-depth study is needed to explain the mecha-nism of poor biomass fractionation efficiency.

Computational studies and theoretical parameters are important to predict the chemical properties of molecular solvents. For example, several empirical and semi-empirical polarity scales have been used to predict the solubility of lignocellulosic biopolymers or the pretreatment efficiency, including the Kamlet–Taft (K-T) solvatochromic method,¹² conductor-like screening models for real solvents,¹³ and Hansen solubility parameters.¹⁴ However, empirical prediction models have some limitations, as they can only predict the results according to the measured data. With the development of computational molecular science, molecular dynamics simulations and quantum calculations have been used to gain a better understanding of the exact mechanism of lignocellulose fractionation in solvents. For example, molecular dynamic simulations have been used to reveal how tetrahydrofuran/water co-solvents interact with the lignocellulose components and contribute to the pretreatment process.¹⁵ The mechanism of the excellent solubility of lignin in ethylene glycol was explained through the quantum calculation of lignin model compounds.¹⁶ Recently, quantum calculation analyses have also been conducted on ChCl-based DESs. Wagle et al. reported different interactions and thermodynamics in three types of ChCl-based DESs. The physical properties could be changed by tuning the choline–Cl⁻ interaction with HBDs.¹⁷ García et al. studied the relationship between the melting point and hydrogen bond (H-bond) networks in 45 types of DESs by a density functional theory (DFT) study and Bader's theory.¹⁸ Li et al. systematically studied the nature of the interactions between ChCl/glycerol DES and SO₂ using DFT calculations. The results showed that SO₂ interacted with both the

hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and HBD through charge- transfer interactions. 19 However, to the best of our knowledge, no theoretical study has been performed on the biomass fractionation properties of ChCl/glycerol DES.

Herein, we try to obtain an in-depth understanding of the intermolecular interactions in ChCl-glycerol DES by studying them through a combination of DFT electronic structure calcu- lations and the K-T solvatochromic parameters. Specifically, we focus on the molecular geometries, charge delocalization effects, and thermochemistry of these systems, exploring a better understanding of "What is important for lignocellulose fractionation using glycerol-based DES?" On the basis of the results, we aim to make full use of the advantage of the design- able diversity of DESs to develop more efficient three-constitu- ent DESs (3c-DESs) for lignin fractionation. 3c-DESs are systematically characterized by several spectroscopic approaches and the K-T solvatochromic parameters, and their lignin extraction ability is tested by applying to poplar wood under different conditions (Scheme 1).

## Lignin fractionation Three identical samples were mixed containing 1 g of poplar wood powder and 20 g DES, and the mixtures were heated in a 50 mL glass bottle at 110, 120, and 130 °C for 4 h each. The resultant dark brown liquid was poured in 200 mL acetone/ water (70:30 v/v) solution and stirred for 2 h. The mixture was vacuum-filtered and washed with the same solution three times. After filtration, the mixture was then heated in a rotary evaporator at 60 °C to remove the acetone. Deionized water was added to the solution to precipitate the dissolved lignin.

## DFT calculations The relevant calculations were carried out with the Gaussian 09 program package. The initial geometry optimizations were obtained using the M06-2X exchange-correlation function combined with the 6-31G* basis set. All samples were subjected to re-optimization at the M06-2X/6-31+G** level. To eliminate the dispersion effect, we added the keyword of empirical dispersion = gd3 in the route section, and all calculations were optimized under no symmetry restrictions. Frequency analysis at the M06-2X/6-31+G** level was performed for the optimized structures to verify energy minima and provide zero-point energy corrections. The thermochemical characteristics were obtained for single-point energy calculations at the M06-2X/6-311++G** level to test their consistency and reproducibility.

The atoms in molecules (AIM) theory was employed to quantify the H-bonding interactions. Based on the AIM theory, the prominent criteria for the assessment of the existence of hydrogen bonds were proposed as follows: the presence of a bond path and an interatomic surface, the existence of the bond critical point (BCP), the range of ρ from 0.002 to 0.035 au, and the scope of Δ²ρ from 0.024 to 0.139 au.

The bond-acceptor-donor interactions were analyzed through 2D (the reduced density gradient S, versus the product of the sign of the second eigenvalue of the Hessian matrix and the electron density, signal (λ₂)ρ) and 3D-NCI (non-covalent interactions) plots. The 2D-NCI plot provides the information on the weak interactions and compares them with strong inter- actions. The 3D-NCI plot shows a three-color code to differen- tiate between attractive interactions (blue), very weak non- covalent interactions (green), and repulsive interactions (red). The darkest shade of blue corresponds to the strongest hydro- gen bond.

**Measurement of the K–T solvatochromic parameters** Nile red was used as a solvatochromic indicator to determine α, and 4-nitroaniline (NH₂) was used to determine β. N,N- Diethyl-4-nitroaniline (NEt₂) was selected to determine π*. See Note S1 in the ESI† for details.

**Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy** FTIR spectra were recorded using a Nicolet Magna 560 instru- ment (Thermo Fisher Corp., USA). The spectra were recorded in attenuated total reflectance mode, and the data were recorded from 650 to 4000 cm⁻¹, with 32 scans per spectrum and a resolution of 4 cm⁻¹.

## Results and discussion ### Investigation of H-bonding interactions in ChCl/glycerol DES by DFT calculation DESs are formed from mixtures containing several anionic, cationic, or nonionic species.20 The properties of DESs vary with different HBA and HBD combinations. The different qualities of H-bonds lead to the difficulties associated with the quantification of H-bonding interactions.21 Here, DFT calculation was employed to gain an insight into the H-bonding interactions of ChCl-glycerol at the atomic level. The molecular structures and optimized conformations of ChCl, glycerol, and the prepared ChCl/glycerol (1:2) DES are shown in Fig. 1. The choline cation (Ch+) may be considered as a tetrahedron formed by the methyl/methylene groups of a quaternary ammonium head and a CH2OH chain extending from one of the vertices and partially blocking the corresponding face (Fig. 1a). Choline can adopt either a _trans_ or _gauche_ conformation with respect to the N-C-C-O torsion angle. Additionally, three hydroxyl groups in the glycerol endow the ChCl-glycerol with numerous H-bond interacting capabilities (Fig. 1b). Thus, the H-bonding interactions in ChCl-glycerol (Fig. 1c) can be identified as: Ch+ and glycerol (cationic H-bond), chloride ion (Cl-) and glycerol (anionic H-bond),

ChCl ion pairs (doubly ionic H-bond), and glycerol–glycerol (neutral H-bond). These interatomic distances are all within the accepted criteria of H-bond coordination (<3.5 Å).²² The distance of Ch⁺ and Cl⁻ delocalization is 0.397 Å, which is plausible to increase the degree of freedom of Cl⁻.

The AIM theory was used to study the critical points between the HBD and HBA nuclei and quantify the H-bond interactions in terms of the electron density (ρ) and the Laplacian of the electron density (∇²ρ) at the bond critical point (BCP).²³ The BCP between two atoms is indicative of a bonding interaction, the ρ value describes the strength of a bond, and the ∇²ρ value indicates the characteristic of a bond (ionic bond, H-bond, or van der Waals bond). The criterion for the existence of an H-bond is a range of 0.002–0.035 au for ρ and 0.024–0.139 au for ∇²ρ.²⁴ Fig. S1 in the ESI† shows a simulated topological graph of ChCl-glycerol, and Table S1† summarizes the values of ρ and ∇²ρ for all BCPs between the HBD and HBA. The positive values of ∇²ρ are all within the H-bond and van der Waals force range. The AIM molecular graphs in Fig. 2a show the strength of the anionic ([Cl(glycerol)]⁻), cationic ([Ch(glycerol)]⁺), and neutral (glycerol–glycerol) H-bonds in ChCl-glycerol. The O₁–H₇···Cl₄₄ H-bond interaction with Cl⁻ is one of the strongest H-bonds, and ρBCP = 0.021 au, which is larger than that of an H-bond interacting mainly with Ch⁺ (ρBCP = 0.014 au). Cl⁻ not only forms stronger H-bonds in Cl-glycerol, it is also circulated by van der Waals, C₁₈–H₂₅···Cl₄₄ ρBCP = 0.005 au, and ∇²ρ = 0.014 au (Table S1 in the ESI†). Hence, the number and strength of anionic H-bonds are greater than those of cationic H-bonds, suggesting that the anionic H-bonds play dominant roles in ChCl-glycerol and manifold anions have actually been occupied by the H-bonds.

The scatter graph from the reduced density gradient analysis shows the corresponding H-bonding interactions, van der Waals bonding, and steric effects. Based on the above theoretical calcu- lations, Cl⁻ was found to be surrounded by glycerol. The ineffi- ciency of ChCl/glycerol DES for biomass fractionation is due to the insufficient HBA ability of ChCl–glycerol to compete with the inner H-bonds in LCCs.

We then calculated the H-bonding strengths in lignin using 1-(4-methoxyphenyl)-2-methoxyethanol as the model com- pound. Lignin has a variety of electron-rich phenylpropanols that are irregularly joined together through C-O and C-C lin- kages to create a complex structural network (Fig. S2, ESI†). The intramolecular H-bonds are mainly OH···O bonds (Fig. 3a). Most of the ρ values are close to 0.022 au (Table S1†). Thus, the H-bonding strengths in ChCl-glycerol are weaker compared to those in lignin (lignin-lignin > Cl⁻-glycerol > Ch⁺-glycerol), suggesting that ChCl/glycerol DES cannot break the H-bonds in lignin. Furthermore, the β-O-4 ether linkage is another common linkage in lignin, which accounts for approximately 50% of all linkages.²⁵ The bond dissociation energies (BDE) of phenethyl phenyl ether (a model of the β-O-

4 ether linkage) for C–O and C–C in Fig. 3b were calculated as 62.25 kcal mol⁻¹ and 76.22 kcal mol⁻¹, respectively, which are both larger than the H-bonding energy of 4.3–40 kcal mol⁻¹. This indicates that the H-bonding energy of the ChCl/glycerol DES was unable to cleave the ether bonds in lignin.

Design of 3c-DES using a multisite coordination strategy Based on the above theoretical calculations, the inefficiency of ChCl/glycerol DES for biomass fractionation was ascribed to the weak H-bond-accepting ability of occupied-site anions and the inadequacy of protons/active acidic sites to cleave the H-bonds and ether bonds in LCCs. Therefore, inspired by the development of a Type IV DES (metal chloride hydrate with HBD), 26 seven types of metal chlorides/metal chloride hydrates were tested to mix with ChCl and glycerol, and a series of ChCl/glycerol/metal chloride solvents were formed (Fig. S3, ESI†). The DESs with hypervalent AlCl3.6H2O exhibited the maximal Lewis acid strength, the most prominent K-T parameters, and the strongest lignin fractionation ability (Table S2, ESI†). The 3c-DESs were analyzed using FTIR and Raman spec- troscopy. The force attenuation of intermolecular and intra- molecular H-bonds in the ChCl/glycerol DES is illustrated by the decrease in the hydroxyl stretching frequency in the region of 3200–3300 cm⁻¹ (Fig. 4a).²⁷ The emergence of a peak at approximately 1700 cm⁻¹ was assigned to the stretching vibration of Al-H, and the signal intensity gradually increased with increasing AlCl₃·6H₂O content. The peak at 2903 cm⁻¹ was assigned to νs(CH₂), and that at 2953 cm⁻¹ was assigned to νas(CH₂),²⁸ which display enhanced asymmetric stretching vibrations once the 3c-DES is formed. This implies that the primary hydroxyls of glycerol are likely to coordinate with AlCl₃·6H₂O because aluminum's three-elec- tron redox properties attract electron-rich oxygen.²⁹ From the ²⁷Al NMR spectra in Fig. 4c, the hydrated metallic salts as ligands can partly control the coordination chemistry around the aluminum center.³⁰ The resonance peaks in the 0–2 ppm range of the 3c-DESs originate from the octahedral hexa-co- ordinated aluminum species.³¹ [Al(OH)₂(H₂O)₄]⁺, which is con- sidered the dominant species of AlCl₃·6H₂O, can coordinate

with glycerol as an unidentate ligand, and this correlation is ascribed to the HO...Alᵛᴵ coordination.³² Alᵛᴵ is bound to gly- cerol by the oxygen atom in the form of [Al(OH)₂(H₂O)₄]⁺ to form [Al(OH)·(H₂O)₄(ligand)]⁺, leading to an upfield shift in the resonance (0–0.7 ppm).

The K-T solvatochromic method served as a quantitative tool to estimate the chemical properties of the 3c-DESs (Fig. S5, ESI†). DESs with a high α value can easily donate H-bonds to liberate H⁺, whereas that with a high β value has a high H-bond-accepting capacity. The α and β values of ChCl/glycerol DES were only 0.77 and 0.48, respectively (Table 1). In contrast, the α values of the 3c-DESs were improved to 1.9–2.0 (Fig. 4d); such high values indicate that it is very easy for them to release H⁺. The β values also increased with the increasing AlCl₃·6H₂O addition and reached up to 0.68. The π* values exhibited a slight decrease. Lignin fractionation using the 3c-DESs Poplar wood powder was treated with the 3c-DESs by heating in an oil bath at 110, 120, and 130 °C for 4 h to verify their lignin fractionation efficiency (Fig. S6, ESI†). The mass percentages of the lignin fractions (LF) and cellulose residues (CR) were calculated (for the calculation methods, see Note S2 in the ESI†) and are listed in Table 2. The results show that the lignin extraction rate (LER) changes with the increasing amount of AlCl3.6H2O and increasing temperatures (Fig. 5a). The yield of LF increases from 0.69 ± 0.21% (using ChCl/glycerol DES treated at 120 °C for 4 h) to 18.2 ± 0.72% using 3c-DES-4 at 120 °C for 4 h, which accounts for 95.46 ± 0.82% of the lignin content in raw wood feedstock (Fig. S7, ESI†). The purity of the 3c-DES-4-extracted lignin (3c-DESL) reached 94 ± 0.45% (for the calculation method, see Note S3 in the ESI†). The 3c-DESL yield at 130 °C exceeds 19.12% (lignin content in raw wood feedstock); such a high value was possibly due to the generation of pseudolignin from carbohydrates (SEM image in Fig. S8 in the ESI†).35 It is also worth noting that when AlCl3.6H2O and glycerol were used to form a Type IV DES (metal chloride hydrate and HBD), the LER could only reach 64.43% (Fig. S9 in ESI†); this result reveals that the H-bond interactions within the ternary DES are of great importance. Fig. 5b shows that the 3c-DESL yield also has a close correlation with the increasing ẞ values, which confirms that high H-bond basicity can increase the capability of the solvent to disrupt the H-bond network.36

To explore the lignin fractionation mechanism of the 3c- DES, the interactions between Clⁱ and the models of mono- meric lignin were analyzed by DFT calculations (Fig. 5c). The results indicate that Clⁱ is likely to form weak H-bonds with CH (CHCl, ρ < 0.015 au) and strong H-bonds with OH

(OH···Cl, 0.028 < ρ < 0.036 au). The H-bonding strength of OH···Cl is higher than that of the OH···O bond in lignin, although O is typically considered as a good HBA. This proves that multisite Cl⁻ is required to compete with lignin to break the H-bond network in lignocellulose. From the previous BDE calcu- lation in Fig. 3b, it is obvious that the weak ether bond (C–O) in lignin is most likely to be cleaved instead of the stronger C–C bond. The possible reaction pathway is shown in Fig. 5d. Firstly, acidolysis occurs in the 3c-DES to form a positive proton at Cα. After the deprotonation and protonation process, a resonance- stabilized positive charge is formed as shown in Fig. 5d(2). Finally, the ether bond is cleaved after the Cβ is hydrated and deprotonated to form ketone and phenol groups.

troscopy characterization and K-T solvatochromic parameters were used. DFT calculation was reasonably used to understand the molecular interactions within the constituent mixtures of ChCl/glycerol DES. An inefficiency mechanism was found due to the weak competing interactions of ChCl-glycerol with the linkages in the LCCs. The Cl¯ in ChCl-glycerol was sur- rounded by mutually anionic H-bonds ([Cl(glycerol)]¯) and cat- ionic H-bonds ([Ch(glycerol)]⁺), which resulted in the weak H-bond-accepting ability of occupied-site anions and inadequate protons/inactive acidic sites. For this reason, the K-T parameters of ChCl/glycerol DES, especially α and β, were significantly smaller than those of powerful DESs. In this regard, a molecular design of a ternary DES was proposed based on an acidic multisite coordination strategy. AlCl₃·6H₂O as an anion donor and active acidic site holder was introduced in ChCl/glycerol. The competition of anionic H-bonds (CH···Cl/OH···Cl) and unidentate aluminum ligands ([Al (OH)·(H₂O)₄(ligand)n]⁺) was synchronized to form chlorine ion-metal cation-HBA supramolecular complexes. The result- ing 3c-DES showed typical “deep” and “eutectic” character- istics. Consequently, the K-T parameters α and β of the 3c-DES significantly increased to 1.99 and 0.68, respectively. The lignin extraction rate using the 3c-DES was improved to 95.46% with a purity of 94%. The reduction of molecular weight and polydispersity ensured that the LF has good charac- teristics for further utilization. In conclusion, this work pre- sents a contribution to the general areas of sustainability of biomass refinery with a specially designed 3c-DES. Such work may also inspire rising research enthusiasm in the exploration of DESs tailored for bio-refinery and bio-transformation.

Multiple hydrogen bond coordination in three-constituent deep eutectic solvents enhances lignin fractionation from biomass <::logo: Royal Society of Chemistry ROYAL SOCIETY OF CHEMISTRY The logo features a stylized 'C' formed by overlapping circular segments in shades of blue, green, and yellow.:> Green Chemistry PAPER View Article Online View Journal | View Issue <::button: Check for updates::> Cite this: Green Chem., 2018, 20, 2711 Multiple hydrogen bond coordination in three- constituent deep eutectic solvents enhances lignin fractionation from biomass† Qinqin Xia, Yongzhuang Liu, Juan Meng, Wanke Cheng, Wenshuai Chen, Shouxin Liu, ID Yixing Liu, Jian Li and Haipeng Yu ID * As an emerging generation of green solvents, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are promising for the pre-treatment of lignocellulose and the production of biochemicals. However, not all DESs are effective for the cleavage of lignin–carbohydrate complexes (LCCs) in lignocellulose and the fractionation of lignin. In this study, we analyzed the nature of complex molecular interactions between choline chloride (ChCl) and glycerol in ChCl/glycerol (1:2) DES using density functional theory and the Kamlet–Taft solvatochro-mic method. The ChCl–glycerol DES exhibited weak competing interactions towards the linkages in the LCC network because the intramolecular hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) in ChCl–glycerol were constrained by mutually anionic H-bonds ([Cl(glycerol)]⁻) and cationic H-bonds ([Ch(glycerol)]⁺). Furthermore, because of the absence of active protons and acidic sites, the DES was unable to cleave ether bond lin-kages in the LCCs. Accordingly, we designed a three-constituent DES (3c-DES) by coordinating AlCl₃·6H₂O in ChCl/glycerol DES based on an acidic multisite coordination theory. The competition of anionic H-bonds and unidentate aluminum ligands was synchronized to form supramolecular complexes, allowing the multisite bridging ligands to cleave both the H-bonds and ether bonds in LCCs. Consequently, the lignin fractionation efficiency was significantly improved from 3.61% to 95.46%, and the lignin purity reached 94 ± 0.45%. Received 21st March 2018, Accepted 22nd April 2018 DOI: 10.1039/c8gc00900g rsc.li/greenchem With the depletion of fossil energy resources, biomass utilization is of significant importance for the production of alternative renewables.¹ Recently, the biomass pretreatment efficiency has been improved with the development and better understanding of novel solvents that do not harm the environment and are compatible with nature.² Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as a promising new generation of green solvents which fully accord with the 12 principles of green chemistry. They are inexpensive, easy to prepare, nontoxic, biodegradable, and environmentally friendly.³ Compared with toxic solvents and expensive solvents, DESs can be used in lieu of conventional chemical solvents and have a low ecological footprint. Some acidic DESs that show an efficient lignin extraction ability have been reported. However, not all types of DESs can be applied to biomass fractionation. DFT calculation was reasonably used to understand the molecular interactions within the constituent mixtures of ChCl/glycerol DES. An inefficiency mechanism was found due to the weak competing interactions of ChCl-glycerol with the linkages in the LCCs. The Cl¯ in ChCl-glycerol was sur- rounded by mutually anionic H-bonds ([Cl(glycerol)]¯) and cat- ionic H-bonds ([Ch(glycerol)]⁺), which resulted in the weak H-bond-accepting ability of occupied-site anions and inadequate protons/inactive acidic sites. For this reason, the K-T parameters of ChCl/glycerol DES, especially α and β, were significantly smaller than those of powerful DESs. In this regard, a molecular design of a ternary DES was proposed based on an acidic multisite coordination strategy. AlCl₃·6H₂O as an anion donor and active acidic site holder was introduced in ChCl/glycerol. The competition of anionic H-bonds (CH···Cl/OH···Cl) and unidentate aluminum ligands ([Al (OH)·(H₂O)₄(ligand)n]⁺) was synchronized to form chlorine ion-metal cation-HBA supramolecular complexes. The result- ing 3c-DES showed typical “deep” and “eutectic” character- istics. Consequently, the K-T parameters α and β of the 3c-DES significantly increased to 1.99 and 0.68, respectively. The lignin extraction rate using the 3c-DES was improved to 95.46% with a purity of 94%. The reduction of molecular weight and polydispersity ensured that the LF has good charac- teristics for further utilization. In conclusion, this work pre- sents a contribution to the general areas of sustainability of biomass refinery with a specially designed 3c-DES. In this study, we analyzed the nature of complex molecular interactions between choline chloride (ChCl) and glycerol in ChCl/glycerol (1:2) DES using density functional theory and the Kamlet–Taft solvatochro-mic method. Furthermore, because of the absence of active protons and acidic sites, the DES was unable to cleave ether bond lin-kages in the LCCs. The competition of anionic H-bonds and unidentate aluminum ligands was synchronized to form supramolecular complexes, allowing the multisite bridging ligands to cleave both the H-bonds and ether bonds in LCCs.
